 6   I. SCOPE OF THE BRIEF AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

 7             No one in this docket needs to be persuaded that the Permian Basin needs power. I work

 8   in high-tech and I build with the tools that are driving this demand, and I agree without

 9   reservation that the basin needs reliable supply. But needing power is not the same as needing

10   this line, on this land, at this price. A project that was first studied at lower voltage grew into the

11   highest-voltage line in Texas, and the cost has kept climbing as it grew. Commission Staff's own

12   witness agreed that the estimate has already moved from about $6.2 million per mile to roughly

13   $7.5 million per mile, a 21 percent increase, and agreed in the same answer that the tariff

14   exposure on steel and aluminum was set aside and never analyzed.1 Add years of inflation and

15   the tariff costs the model leaves out, and that number rises again. A line that takes private land,

16   introduces fire risk across fifteen counties, and keeps growing in cost is not automatically the

17   right way to deliver reliable power to the basin, and the burden to show that it is rests with the

18   Applicants. Whether this project is the necessary answer to that need is itself contested before the

19   Commission. The question of need is common to the Permian Basin 765-kV proceedings, and a

20   motion is pending to reserve that common need determination until the supply and generation

21   that would justify it are established. I have supported that motion, and members of the Texas

  2   Legislature have addressed it as well.2 This brief does not relitigate the need. It addresses routing

 3   in case the Commission moves forward, and it raises the narrower, more practical question the

 5   gets built run through Link F20 and Link F23, or should it not?

 6          The answer comes down to a single decision the Administrative Law Judges are well

 7   equipped to make. The Applicants' own witnesses divided the routing factors into two kinds.

 8   Some impacts can be cured after the route is chosen, by moving a structure or adjusting a span.

 9   Other impacts are fixed the moment a link is selected and cannot be engineered away. The route

10   should be chosen on the factors the route choice actually controls.

11          When the Commission applies that decision rule, the result does not depend on whose

12   philosophy it adopts. There are two reasonable ways to weigh the factors, and both lead away

13   from F20.

14          Under the first approach, the Commission gives controlling weight to the factors that

15   cannot be cured by engineering: habitable structures and the prudent avoidance that rides on

16   them, the level of community opposition, the amount of compatible right-of-way the route can

18   and 296, better satisfy the Commission's criteria, and the neutral party in this case, Commission

19   Staff, has already recommended a route other than 894 on one of those very factors.

20          Under the second approach, the Commission credits every factor, including the ones an

21   engineer can address. Even then, a route exists that keeps the entire alignment of the preferred

22   route except the Bell County segment at issue, ties that route on the factor the Applicants

 8   II. STATEMENT OF INTEREST AND BACKGROUND

 9            I own and live on approximately 19.75 acres at 12808 FM 2843 in Salado, Bell County,

10   Texas. My family has worked this land as a cattle ranch for 22 years. Our sole source of water,

11   for the house and for the livestock, is a well into the Trinity Aquifer.3 My father, Aaron Edward

12   Howton, owns the adjoining property between mine and the proposed line, and he has filed his

13   own direct testimony in this docket.4

14            Link F20 runs along the Cedar Valley corridor a short distance east of my property. Link

15   F23 carries the proposed Route 894 across the area to the north. From my property I will be able

16   to see four of the contested Bell County links: F20, F23, F22, and F21. F22 sits the furthest

17   across an endangered species habitat area and is the hardest to see directly, but I can see across

18   the top of the cedar and oak groves to the home of my neighbor Verlon Tweedle, which sits next

19   to it, so I will see that segment of the corridor as well. The highest-voltage line in Texas, on

20   structures up to 198 feet tall in a 200-foot right-of-way, would be a fixed feature of the view

21   from the land my family has worked for 22 years. I oppose Links F20 and F23 in every route in

22   which they appear.

 7   III. THE GOVERNING STANDARD

 8            The Commission may amend a certificate only after considering the factors set out in

 9   PURA Section 37.056(c)(4): community values, recreational and park areas, historical and

10   aesthetic values, and environmental integrity. The Commission's routing rule, 16 Texas

11   Administrative Code Section 25.101(b)(3)(B), directs that lines be routed, to the extent

12   reasonable, to parallel compatible right-of-way, to parallel property lines and natural or cultural

13   features, and to conform to the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance.

14            Two principles govern how those factors are applied here.

15            First, the Applicants' preferred route carries no special weight. The Commission may

16   certificate any route made up of the filed links, whether or not the Applicants prefer it. The

17   guidance to unrepresented parties in this docket states the rule plainly: the Applicants' preferred

18   route carries no special weight in the analysis, and any route consisting of identified links may be

19   recommended and approved.6

20            Second, prudent avoidance in this case is not an abstract idea, and it is not my reading of

21   the rule. The Applicants' own witnesses defined it. They testified that prudent avoidance is

22   implemented through the structure configuration and the 200-foot right-of-way width that govern

  2   the electric and magnetic fields a person near the line would experience.7 And they described the

 3   Commission's inquiry as turning on the policy of prudent avoidance and the habitable structures,

 4   and the type of habitable structures, a route runs near.8 A former Chairman of this Commission

 5   gave the rule the same meaning under oath. Barry T. Smitherman, former Chairman of the Public

 6   Utility Commission and the Railroad Commission of Texas, testified that prudent avoidance

 7   under 16 TAC Section 25.101 is about limiting human exposure to electric and magnetic fields

 8   that can be avoided with a reasonable investment of money and effort, that it is about exposure to

 9   people rather than to a structure or its foundation or roof, and that the habitable structure count is

10   used as a proxy for the number of humans a route affects.9 So, the definition is neither contested

11   nor mine. The Applicants apply it, and a former Chairman of the deciding agency confirmed it.

12   Prudent avoidance is a question about people in structures near the line, which ties it to the

13   habitable structure count, and as shown below, the habitable structure count is fixed by the link.


14   IV. THE DISPOSITIVE QUESTION: WHICH FACTORS THE ROUTE CHOICE

15   ACTUALLY CONTROLS

16          The routing factors are not all the same kind of thing, and once you see the difference,

17   this case has a clean decision rule. The Applicants' own two witnesses drew that difference

18   themselves, one right after the other, on cross-examination.

19          Some impacts can be fixed after the route is chosen. Ms. Cooley, the Applicants'

20   engineering witness, testified that stream and river crossings can be built from opposite banks to

21   avoid placing fill, that structures are set as far from sensitive features as possible, and that with

22   the project's typical 1,400 to 1,500 foot spans the line can span most crossings, including the

  2   Colorado River, with minimal to no impact.10 In other words, how much a stream crossing, a

 3   riparian corridor, or a wetland gets disturbed depends on how the line is engineered, not on

 4   which link the route uses. And these are exactly the factors where Route 894 holds its slim lead.

 5   They are also exactly the factors an engineer can address on whatever route the Commission

 6   picks.

 7             Other impacts are locked in the moment a link is chosen. Mr. Marusak, the

 8   Applicants' routing witness, confirmed that nudging a structure within the right-of-way is a

 9   single-structure, single-property fix, and that it does not move the line off a densely settled area

10   or meaningfully lower a link's habitable structure count.11 Put Link F20 in the route, and the

11   homes along F20 are in the route. No span adjustment makes them go away.

12             The same is true of the other factors that the link sets and no engineer can undo. How

13   much compatible right-of-way a route can paralleling is fixed by the links it uses. How much

14   community opposition it draws is fixed by whose land it crosses. And cost is set by the link's

15   length, terrain, and the structures it requires.

16             So, the decision rule writes itself. A factor that engineering can fix should not decide

17   which link to use, because the fix is available either way. A factor that the link locks in should

18   carry the weight, because the link choice is the only chance to deal with it.

19             This is not a rule I invented and asked the Commission to adopt. It is the line the

20   Applicants' own witnesses drew under oath. The two sections that follow apply that rule the two

21   ways a reasonable decision-maker might, and both land on a route without Link F20.

  2   V. FIRST PATH: ON THE FACTORS THE ROUTE CHOICE CONTROLS, ROUTES

 3   295 AND 296 BETTER SATISFY THE COMMISSION'S CRITERIA AND AVOID THE

 4   CORRIDOR ENTIRELY

 5           The first path gives the weight to the factors the link locks in and engineering cannot fix:

 6   habitable structures and the prudent avoidance tied to them, community opposition, compatible

 7   right-of-way, and cost. The record shows these are the factors that actually drive Commission

 8   route decisions. Weigh them, and Routes 295 and 296 are the better choice.

 9           Both the Applicants and Staff agree these are the factors that matter. The

10   Applicants' witness Ms. Perkins testified that the strengths she cited for Route 894 were length,

11   cost, and habitable structures, and agreed those are the factors the Commission has looked at in

12   past dockets and that they are important.12 Staff's witness, Mr. Poole, testified that the strengths

13   of his recommended Route 487 were cost, compatible right-of-way paralleling, and habitable

14   structures, and agreed that both Staff and the Applicants found cost and habitable structures to be

15   significant.13 So, three of the four factors I call route-determinative, cost, habitable structures,

16   and compatible right-of-way, are the exact factors both sides put at the center of the case.

17           Staff, the neutral party, already recommended against Route 894 on one of these

18   factors. Mr. Poole recommended Route 487 over Route 894, and testified that more paralleling

19   of compatible right-of-way was one of his primary reasons.14 Compatible right-of-way is a route-

20   determinative factor. And on it, the one party in this case with no financial stake in the outcome

21   concluded that a route other than 894 is better.

 4             This is, at bottom, a total landed cost problem, and it is the part of cost estimation I do for

 5   a living. Ms. Cooley confirmed two things that, taken together, decide the issue. The estimates

 6   for all 122 routes carry no line item for the Section 232 tariffs on steel or aluminum, including

 7   the April 2026 tariffs, and the pricing assumes imported steel structures and imported large-

 8   power transformers.25 That is a purchase-price-at-time-of-estimate figure, not a landed cost. The

 9   difference matters because a tariff is levied on the value of the imported steel, so the tariff burden

10   scales with the tonnage of steel a route requires. It is not a flat percentage spread evenly across

11   every route. A route loaded with full-tension dead-end structures carries more steel per mile, and

12   therefore more dutiable value per mile, than a route built mostly of tangent towers. The exposure

13   is route-dependent by its nature. Mr. Poole's own numbers show the direction of travel: the per-

14   mile estimate has already moved from about $6.2 million to roughly $7.5 million, a 21 percent

15   jump, with the tariff exposure on steel and aluminum set aside and never analyzed.26 So, the

16   model fails on cost twice over. It is blind to structure type, and it omits the one input, tariffed

17   imported steel, whose burden rises precisely on the routes that carry more of the heavy

18   structures. Both failures run in the same direction, and both understate the cost of the structure-

19   heavy route.

 5   VI. SECOND PATH: CREDITING EVERY FACTOR, ROUTES 899 AND 499 REMOVE

 6   F20 AND F23 WHILE CHANGING NOTHING ELSE

 7           If the Commission would rather credit every factor, even the ones an engineer can fix, the

 8   answer comes out the same. The fight in this case is confined to one stretch, the Bell County F-

 9   segment. East of it, the route runs through Cedar Valley on F20 and F23. West of it, nobody

10   disputes the alignment. That makes a surgical fix possible. A route exists that keeps the entire

11   alignment of the preferred route, the Colorado River crossing and everything west of it, and

12   changes only the Bell County F-segment to take out F20 and F23.

13           For the Applicants' own Route 894, that route is Route 899. The two share every link

14   except the F-segment. Route 894 runs F31-F32-F20-F23 through Cedar Valley. Route 899 runs

15   F21-E9-G71 instead, then rejoins the identical alignment and holds it all the way to the end, river

16   crossing included. For Staff's recommended Route 487, the match is Route 499, which makes the

17   same single swap and keeps the rest of Staff's preferred alignment. So, whichever western route

18   the Commission likes, the Applicants' or Staff's, there is a version of it that removes the

19   contested links and disturbs nothing else.

20           Route 899 matches Route 894 on habitable structures as reported, and it removes

21   the contested links. The Applicants' routing witness confirmed that Routes 894, 898, and 899

22   each have 85 habitable structures within 500 feet, and that Route 899 avoids Link F20 and Link

 5   structures, avoids F20 and F23, runs shorter, and costs no more. Ms. Perkins did not dispute a
